messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Children Present: Being around children, Media / News: Related news, Known People: Related people
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Yousef was a 78-year-old Middle Eastern man who had spent most of his adult life working as a roofer, a job he took pride in because it kept him busy, allowed him to support his family, and, in his words, “put me up high where I can think.” He had been married for many years and lived a life that was, until the trauma, structured by work, home, and extended family contact. Several years earlier, while on a roofing project, he had been exposed to a toxic chemical in a way that felt sudden, disorienting, and beyond his control. He did not describe the event with much detail at first, saying only that one moment he was doing the work he knew, and the next his body was reacting to something on the roof that should not have been there. What stayed with him was the sense that the exposure had entered him unexpectedly and that he had been left to get through the day while carrying an invisible danger inside his own body.

In the months that followed, Yousef noticed that certain situations began to unsettle him in a way that felt immediate and bodily. Being around children, which had once been ordinary and even pleasurable through his grandchildren and relatives, now made him tense and watchful. He could not easily explain it to himself, only that their presence brought back a sense of vulnerability and made him feel exposed. He also found that related news reports could catch him off guard; if television or radio coverage mentioned incidents involving chemicals or contamination, he would feel a sharp tightening inside and often leave the room without finishing the story. Even hearing about people who knew of similar events, or seeing someone connected to such a situation, could stir the same reaction. He did not like how quickly these moments got under his skin, and he began to arrange his days to avoid them when possible.

At home and elsewhere, Yousef became increasingly aware that his body would react before he had time to think. If someone touched him unexpectedly, even a light touch from behind or a hand on his shoulder, he would react with alarm, his whole body jolting as if he had been startled into danger. He found himself unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, including in his own house. Sitting in the living room, he could tell himself that nothing was happening, that he was with his wife and that the day was ordinary, yet his muscles remained tight and his attention stayed on edge. Nights were difficult in a different way. He had trouble falling asleep, and when sleep came it did not always stay; he would wake and then lie there alert and restless, his mind unwilling to settle. He described these nights as long and watchful, with little sense of rest even when he had done nothing all day.

His relationship to the memory itself was also changed. When he tried to deliberately remember what had happened on the roof, he found it difficult to access the memory in any orderly way. It felt as though the details were sealed off from him when he reached for them. At other times, however, the memory forced its way into his mind when he did not want it to, arriving abruptly and without invitation. He would be doing something ordinary and then find himself overwhelmed by the event’s emotional force. Sometimes what came first was not a clear picture at all, but the full emotional intensity of the experience, as if his body knew what had happened before his mind could assemble the scene. In those moments he felt the same fear and helplessness he associated with the exposure, even when he could not summon a complete image.

Over time, these experiences changed the rhythm of his daily life. At work, he became more guarded about what he could tolerate around him, and in family settings he was less comfortable than before, especially when children were present or when conversation turned to related incidents in the news. His wife had noticed that he sat more tensely and slept poorly, and that he seemed to carry a constant readiness for something to happen. Yousef had not sought help immediately because he was accustomed to handling hardship on his own and hoped the reactions would settle with time. Instead, they persisted and remained distressing, and he eventually came to treatment because he was tired of feeling alarmed by ordinary contact, tired of lying awake night after night, and frightened by the way the memory could seize him without warning. What he wanted most was to feel safe in his own home again and to be able to meet daily life, even with children nearby or a brief touch from someone he trusted, without his body reacting as if the danger were happening all over again.
